Four Years After Historic UN Biodiversity Deal, Global Targets Face Severe Implementation Gaps

Four Years On: Assessing the Montreal Biodiversity Agreement

Four years after nearly every government on Earth signed a landmark agreement in Montreal to halt and reverse the destruction of the natural world, international negotiators are gathering for the Cop17 summit in Yerevan, Armenia. The meeting confronts a sobering reality: despite high-level commitments made at the end of 2022, countries are currently on track to miss nearly all of the deal’s core targets.

The global framework, established under the UN biodiversity convention created at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, set out ambitious goals. These included formally protecting 30% of the planet's land and oceans for nature, restoring nearly a third of degraded ecosystems, and reforming at least $500bn in environmentally harmful subsidies by the end of the decade. However, reports released ahead of Cop17 indicate that tangible progress remains limited, continuing a historical pattern where formal UN nature targets have routinely fallen short of full implementation.

Domestic Challenges and Funding Shortfalls

The gap between political rhetoric and on-the-ground action has drawn sharp criticism from conservation experts worldwide. In the UK, which positioned itself as a vocal advocate during the Montreal negotiations, analysts note that the country is currently tracking to meet only three of the 23 established targets by the end of the decade. Domestic policy shifts—such as adjusted rules on biodiversity net gain, funding reductions for certain international rainforest protection schemes, and debates over marine protections—have highlighted the friction between international pledges and local execution.

Financial commitments have faced similar hurdles. While governments previously agreed to scale up biodiversity finance to $30bn annually by the end of the decade, subsequent shifts in national priorities and foreign aid budgets have constrained spending. In the United States, administration changes and reductions in agency funding have altered the landscape for international conservation projects. Meanwhile, attempts to mobilize private-sector financing—including a newly established fund designed to capture commercial contributions from digital sequences of biodiversity—have generated only modest initial returns.

Political Backlash and Competing Pressures

Efforts to implement the required environmental reforms have frequently intersected with intense political debates. Across Europe, stringent policies aimed at tackling agricultural pollution and nitrogen runoff have sparked widespread protests among farmers and triggered resistance within legislative bodies. Observers note that complex ecological policies are frequently vulnerable to political polarization and oversimplification in public discourse, complicating efforts to enact long-term systemic changes.

Despite these hurdles, experts point to areas of progress. A majority of nations have advanced elements of the agreement, with certain regions nearing the land portion of the 30x30 protection target through the formalization of Indigenous territories and the creation of large-scale marine parks. Rewilding initiatives in countries like Kazakhstan further demonstrate that targeted interventions can yield tangible ecological benefits.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers seeking to understand the ongoing developments at Cop17 and evaluate the factual basis of these international negotiations can review official documentation and updates provided by the United Nations environment frameworks.

  • What is Confirmed: Governments formally adopted the global biodiversity framework in late 2022; current pre-Cop17 assessments indicate that implementation speeds across multiple indicators are lagging behind initial timelines; and ongoing discussions in Armenia center on bridging the delivery gap.
  • What Remains Uncertain: The extent to which individual nations will successfully revise their domestic policy measures, secure long-term public and private funding streams, and resolve political opposition surrounding land-use and subsidy reforms over the remainder of the decade.
  • How to Verify: Readers can access full reports, daily summaries, and official press releases regarding the summit via the original reporting and analysis published by The Guardian's Environment Section.
